newsitem.title: INDIA: India needs to hike oil prices - analysts.
newsitem.headline: India needs to hike oil prices - analysts.

text.p: India, faced with a rising oil import bill and shortfall in domestic output, would need to hike petroleum product prices to offset the impact of a spurt in world crude prices, analysts said on Wednesday.
But government officials ruled out any immediate moves to increase prices of petroleum products.
Officials and analysts estimate India's oil import bill for 1996/97 (April-March) at $9.3 billion against initial projections of $7.6 billion mainly due to a sharp rise in world crude prices.
"The oil import bill will go up. The Oil Coordination Committee has submitted details to the petroleum ministry," an oil ministry official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.
"The oil import bill will definitely be more than $9.0 billion compared to earlier estimates of close to $7.0 billion," said Rajendra Pachouri, head of the independent Tata Energy Research Institute.
The government had estimated world crude oil prices would hover around $18 per barrel but they are now around $26 per barrel, said Sanjiv Patni, analyst with securities firm W.I. Carr.

"The oil prices have gone over and above the government estimates by about $7.0 per barrel and if we average an $3.5-4.0 increase, for the whole year the pressure on the oil pool account will be $1.0 billion," Patni said.

India's annual oil import demand is about 22 to 23 million tonnes (440,000-460,000 barrels per day) of crude and 16 million tonnes (320,000 bpd) of refined products costing around $6.5 billion last year. This accounted for about 20 to 22 percent of the country's total import bill.
India's oil pool deficit, effectively the net subsidy for oil products, for the year to next March 31 was earlier estimated at 55 to 60 billion rupees ($1.54 billion to $1.68 billion).
Newspapers said ministry officials now estimate the deficit to cross $130 billion rupees and discussions were on with the finance ministry on measures to contain the deficit.
Oil prices in India are controlled by the government. Under an "oil pool account mechanism", the state subsidises the price of imported crude sold to refineries.
"They will have to increase the domestic petroleum prices. It is an economic necessity," said Patni.
Patni expected increases in the prices of diesel and kerosene.
"We have to increase diesel prices....," said Pachouri.
But government officials said there was no move to increase prices of petroleum products.
"At the moment the ministry is not contemplating it," said one oil ministry official.
Newspapers said discussions were on in the government to lower customs tariffs on petroleum products to offset the impact of the sharp spurt in global crude prices.

India's domestic crude oil output in 1996/97 was also likely to fall. The chairman of the Oil Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) Bikash Bora said in September that its crude oil output in 1996/97 was expected to drop to 29.2 million tonnes (584,000 bpd) from 31.9 million (638,000 bpd) last year.
